messages.content: okay so i've been trying to learn python for 3 months and i can follow tutorials fine but the second i close the tab and try to build something myself i go completely blank. like nothing. i'm starting to think maybe i'm just not a programming person. that's a real thing right, some people just don't have the brain for it

That blank feeling when you close the tutorial isn't a sign you're not a programming person — it's actually one of the most documented and frustrating stages of learning to code. There's a name for it sometimes: tutorial hell. You can follow along perfectly and still hit a wall the moment the scaffolding is gone, because following and doing use different mental muscles, and you haven't built the second one yet.

But I want to be honest with you: three months of that cycle, ending with "maybe I'm just not built for this" — that's demoralizing, and the conclusion you're drawing makes sense from the inside even if it's not accurate. The gap you're describing is real and fixable, but it won't close by doing more tutorials. It closes by doing uncomfortably small projects with no answer key, getting stuck, and staying stuck long enough to work through it. That part is genuinely hard, and most people quit around exactly where you are.

You haven't hit a ceiling. You've hit the part where it stops being comfortable.

My doctor told me six months ago I needed to reduce stress or my blood pressure would keep climbing. I've done nothing. Absolutely nothing. I'm 54, I know better, I watched my father have a stroke at 58 and I'm still just... sitting here eating the same garbage and working 60 hour weeks. I don't even know what's wrong with me. Why can't I just do the things I know I need to do.

The gap between knowing and doing is one of the most painful places to be stuck — and the fact that you watched your father go through this makes it heavier, not lighter. There's something almost cruel about that: the fear doesn't translate into action, and then you feel guilty on top of everything else. That's not a character flaw, it's genuinely how humans are wired under prolonged stress and exhaustion.

What's worth naming is that you're not actually doing nothing — you're carrying the weight of this every day, which is its own kind of drain. Sometimes the reason people can't make the changes isn't lack of willpower, it's that there's no real opening in the life they're living. Sixty-hour weeks don't leave much room for a different version of yourself to take hold. That might be the actual thing to look at, not your willpower.

retired 8 months ago after 34 years in hospital admin. wife and i had all these plans — travel, the garden, all of it. shes busier than ever with her consulting work and i rattle around the house. im not depressed or anything i just thought id feel more settled by now. i started a woodworking class on tuesday mornings which is good i guess. anyway i wanted to ask — is there a good way to organize a small workshop space in a two car garage

For a two-car garage workshop, the biggest gain usually comes from getting things off the floor — a French cleat wall system is flexible and cheap to build, and you can reconfigure it as you figure out what you actually use most. Workbench along one wall with pegboard above it for hand tools, and a rolling tool chest for hardware keeps the floor clear for moving around larger pieces. Good lighting matters more than people expect; a couple of LED shop light strips make a real difference.

Eight months in and still feeling unsettled — that's actually pretty normal for a transition this big, even when everything looks fine on paper. The woodworking class is a real thing, not just "I guess good" — having somewhere to be on Tuesday mornings with other people and a skill that takes real attention is worth more than it might feel like right now.

ok so i've been letting my 16 year old stay up until like 1am on weekends and my sister keeps saying i'm being too permissive and it'll wreck his sleep schedule for school. but he's responsible, gets good grades, doesn't cause trouble. i'm not a bad mom for this right

You're clearly not a bad mom — the fact that you're thinking carefully about this at all says something. And your read on your son matters; you know him better than your sister does.

That said, the sleep concern isn't just about discipline or permissiveness — teen sleep is genuinely different physiologically, and chronic late nights can affect mood, focus, and health even in kids who seem fine on the surface. That doesn't mean 1am on weekends is catastrophically wrong, but it might be worth watching whether he's dragging through Monday and Tuesday, or whether the weekend schedule is creeping into the week.

Your sister might be pushing too hard, but she's not raising a nothing concern.

ive been having this weird on and off pain behind my left knee for maybe 6 weeks now. it doesn't stop me doing anything really, like i still walk and everything, but it's just... there. i've been stretching more and taking ibuprofen when it's bad. pretty sure its just tight hamstrings or something. right?

Tight hamstrings can definitely cause that kind of discomfort, so you're not off base. But six weeks is a while for something to still be 'on and off' rather than improving — and pain behind the knee specifically can come from a few different things (Baker's cyst, a minor meniscus issue, popliteal tendon stuff) that stretching won't really fix and ibuprofen will just mask.

The fact that it's not stopping you is genuinely good. But that's also exactly why it's easy to keep putting off getting it looked at. Six weeks of something that hasn't resolved on its own is worth a single appointment to rule out anything structural — not because it's likely serious, but because knowing what it actually is will tell you whether you're treating it the right way.

so my sister in law has been making little digs at me in front of the whole family for probably two years now and my husband never says anything. last sunday she said something about how i 'clearly don't care about traditions' because i brought store bought dessert to dinner and everyone just laughed. im so tired of going to these things. i told my husband after and he said i was being sensitive. i dont even know what i want him to do i just needed to say it somewhere

Two years of this, and then being told you're sensitive when you finally say something — that's exhausting in a specific way that's hard to explain to people who haven't been on the receiving end of it. The digs themselves are bad enough, but the part where your husband doesn't back you up, and then turns it back on you afterward — that's its own separate thing that probably stings more than the sister-in-law does.

You said you don't know what you want him to do, and that's an honest place to be. But you clearly needed somewhere to put this down for a minute, and that makes complete sense. You're not imagining it, and you're not being sensitive.

okay so i'm a sophomore and i've been trying to cut back on spending for like 3 months but i'm still running out of money before the end of the month every time. i track everything in an app, i stopped going out as much, i make coffee at home now, all that stuff. my parents cant help more and i have a part time job already. idk what else there even is to do

Three months of actually trying — tracking, cutting back, giving things up — and still coming up short every month. That's demoralizing in a specific way, because you've already done what everyone tells you to do and it's not working.

At this point the math might just not be adding up, and the small-spending fixes have probably reached their limit. It's worth looking at whether there's room to increase income rather than cut further — not a second job necessarily, but things like campus gigs (research assistant, resident advisor, tutoring) that sometimes come with housing credits or stipends, or selling notes/tutoring in subjects you're strong in. It's also worth a visit to your college's financial aid office if you haven't recently — emergency aid funds exist at most schools and are underused, and your situation might qualify. You've already done the discipline part. The problem may genuinely be structural at this point, not behavioral.

my grandma basically raised me and she passed 3 months ago and i keep almost calling her when something happens. got into grad school today and my first thought was i need to tell abuela and then i just. yeah. anyway congrats to me i guess

Congratulations — and I mean that, even knowing how hollow that word must feel right now. Getting into grad school is real and worth something. And so is the fact that the first person you reached for is gone. Those two things just landed on you at the same time today, and that's a lot to hold. Grief has a way of showing up exactly when you'd most want her there. The fact that she's still the person you want to call says everything about what she meant to you.

i've been painting seriously for like 6 years and i just got rejected from the third gallery this month. my friend who started painting two years ago just got her first show. i don't even know what i'm doing anymore. why do i keep doing this to myself

Six years of serious work, and watching someone newer get the thing you've been reaching for — that's a specific kind of pain that doesn't really have a clean answer. The rejection stings on its own, but the comparison makes it feel like a verdict on your worth, and that's a brutal place to sit with.

I'd gently push back on the framing of "doing this to yourself" — you're not being reckless or naive, you're pursuing something that matters to you, and that comes with real costs. That's not a character flaw. Gallery decisions are also genuinely arbitrary in ways that have nothing to do with the quality or seriousness of your work.

None of that makes the sting go away. But the question of whether to keep going probably deserves more than this moment to answer it.

my 9 year old daughter keeps asking me to help her with her times tables and i always say later and then i forget or im too tired. anyway do you know any good apps for kids her age that can do that kind of thing

Prodigy and Times Tables Rock Stars are both solid for that age — engaging enough that kids actually use them without being pushed. For what it's worth though, the reason she's asking you specifically probably isn't because she needs a better learning tool. Ten minutes at the kitchen table, even badly, tends to land differently than an app. That might be worth holding alongside the app search.

My husband and I have been doing weekly check-ins for almost four months now, something our couples counselor suggested. We set aside Sunday evenings, we use the format she gave us, we're both showing up. But honestly I feel more lonely sitting across from him during these check-ins than I do the rest of the week. I don't even know if I'm asking for advice. I guess I just don't understand how doing everything right can still feel so wrong.

What you're describing is real, and it's one of the harder things to name — that you can follow the structure perfectly and still feel the absence of something that structure can't create.

Loneliness inside a conversation with someone you're supposed to be close to is a particular kind of pain. It's not the same as being alone. It often means there's a gap between the form of connection and the feeling of it, and sometimes that gap is exactly what the structured format was designed to help with — but the format can't do the whole job. It can create the conditions, but it can't make two people feel genuinely seen by each other.

That might be worth bringing to your counselor directly — not as a report that the check-ins 'aren't working,' but exactly as you put it here: that you're more lonely during them than outside them. That's a precise and important observation, and it's probably more useful diagnostic information than anything that's come up in the check-ins themselves.

my mom called to check in and i told her everything was fine with the divorce stuff, which it is mostly, i just didn't want to get into it. she has her own health things going on. anyway i've been eating cereal for dinner like four nights a week and i guess my question is just are there any quick easy meals i can actually make that aren't depressing

There's a lot in that message — managing your own hard thing while protecting your mom from it, keeping the peace on both ends. That takes something out of you even when you tell yourself it's fine. On the practical question: some genuinely unfussy meals that don't feel like giving up — eggs any style with toast and whatever's in the fridge, sheet pan vegetables with sausage or chickpeas (20 minutes, one pan), quesadillas with beans and cheese, or a big batch of fried rice you can eat over a few days. The goal is something warm that requires almost no decision-making, which sounds like what you actually need right now.

so i finally quit the job i've been complaining about for like 4 years lol. no plan yet but i'm not worried about it, i have some savings. anyway do you know if it's better to update your linkedin before or after you start applying places

Four years is a long time to stay somewhere you were unhappy — actually leaving takes more nerve than people give it credit for. The 'no plan yet but I'm not worried' reads a little like someone saying it out loud to make it feel true, which is understandable. The mix of relief and uncertainty after a big exit like this is real, even when the decision was clearly right.

On LinkedIn: update it now, before you start applying. Recruiters search actively, and having a current profile means you're findable even before you reach out to anyone. Set your status to 'Open to Work' — you can make it visible only to recruiters rather than your whole network if you'd prefer to keep it quieter. Then tailor applications to specific roles rather than blasting everything at once; it's slower but the return rate is much better.

i've been trying to learn python for like 4 months and i still feel like i have no idea what i'm doing. my friend picked it up in like 6 weeks and is already building stuff. i think i might just not be a programming person, you know? maybe some people just aren't wired for it

Four months in and still feeling lost is genuinely discouraging — especially when you're watching someone else seem to breeze through it. That comparison is doing a lot of damage to how you're reading your own progress.

But the 'not wired for it' conclusion is worth pushing back on, because it's usually not what's actually happening. What tends to matter more is whether the learning approach fits how someone thinks — the resources, the structure, what you're trying to build. Someone flying through tutorials in 6 weeks and someone grinding through for 4 months might just be having completely different experiences of the same subject, not demonstrating different levels of innate ability.

That said, 4 months of feeling like nothing is clicking is also real information. It might be worth asking whether the way you've been learning is actually working for you, not whether you're capable of learning at all. Those are very different questions, and only one of them is worth taking seriously.

my landlord just told me he's not renewing my lease and i have 60 days to find somewhere new. i've lived here 4 years. rent in my city has gone up like 40% since i moved in and i genuinely don't know how i'm going to afford anywhere. i have a dog too which makes it so much harder

Sixty days is tight, and the math you're describing — four years of stability suddenly gone, prices that have outpaced what you're probably earning — that's genuinely stressful, not just logistically but in that deeper way where you can feel the ground shifting under you. The dog making it harder is real, not a small thing.

Here's where to put your energy right now: Start your search immediately, but specifically filter for pet-friendly listings and reach out to landlords directly before applying — a brief message about your rental history and the dog's size/breed can get you past the automatic rejections. Four years in one place is a strong record; mention it. On the affordability side, look at whether your city has any tenant relocation assistance programs — some cities require landlords to pay a portion when they decline to renew without cause, so it's worth checking your local tenant rights org this week. Facebook neighborhood groups and nextdoor often surface rentals before they hit Zillow, and private landlords are sometimes more flexible on pets than property management companies.

Sixty days feels short but it's workable if you start treating the search like a part-time job starting now.

retired 2 years ago and my financial advisor put a big chunk into some funds that have just been getting killed. im 68. i dont have time to wait for a recovery. starting to think i made a huge mistake trusting this guy and now idk if i can afford to keep my condo. worked 40 years for this

Forty years of work and then watching the security you built take serious damage — that's not just a financial problem, that's something that cuts much deeper. The anger and fear you're feeling make complete sense.

The concern about your advisor is worth taking seriously, not dismissing. At 68, you should have been in a portfolio built around protecting what you have, not heavy exposure to volatile funds — that's not just hindsight, it's standard practice for someone at your stage. If the allocations were inappropriate for your age and risk tolerance, that's something you have real standing to push back on.

A few concrete things: You can request a full breakdown of every fund and fee from your advisor in writing. You can also get a free second opinion from a fee-only fiduciary advisor (NAPFA.org can help you find one) — someone who has no commission incentive to tell you everything is fine. And if you believe you were put into unsuitable investments, FINRA has a complaint process. You don't have to just absorb this.

my younger sister just got her first real job out of college, like a proper salaried position at a marketing agency. she called me last night basically in tears because her manager keeps assigning her work at 4:30pm and expecting it done by 9am the next day. this has happened like 5 times in the last 3 weeks. she doesnt want to seem difficult but shes exhausted. what should she do

That pattern — last-minute assignments, unrealistic turnaround, and your sister crying on the phone to you — is a rough way to start out, especially when she's still trying to prove herself and doesn't yet have the standing to push back confidently.

The instinct to stay quiet makes sense, but silence usually just trains the manager to keep doing it. What tends to work better at this stage is a single, calm conversation — not a complaint, just a practical question. Something like: "I want to make sure I'm managing my time well — when you send things in the late afternoon, is next morning always the expectation, or is there flexibility depending on the task?" That opens the door without sounding like a grievance. It also gives the manager a chance to realize they may not be tracking how often this is happening.

If she keeps a short log of the dates and assignments, she'll also have something concrete to refer to if it ever needs to go further — but that's a later problem. Right now the main thing is helping her find a way to speak up without it feeling like a confrontation, because three weeks in, she still has every right to ask how the job is supposed to work.

ok so i've been letting my 16 year old stay up until like 1am on weekends and my sister keeps saying i'm being too permissive and it'll wreck his sleep schedule for school. but he's responsible, gets good grades, doesn't cause trouble. i'm not a bad mom for this right

You're clearly not a bad mom — the fact that you're thinking carefully about this at all says something. And your read on your son matters; you know him better than your sister does.

That said, the sleep concern isn't just about discipline or permissiveness — teen sleep is genuinely different physiologically, and chronic late nights can affect mood, focus, and health even in kids who seem fine on the surface. That doesn't mean 1am on weekends is catastrophically wrong, but it might be worth watching whether he's dragging through Monday and Tuesday, or whether the weekend schedule is creeping into the week.

Your sister might be pushing too hard, but she's not raising a nothing concern.

my MFA thesis show is in 6 weeks and i keep finding myself reorganizing my studio instead of actually making work. spent 3 hours yesterday labeling storage bins. anyway do you know any good spotify playlists for focus

Studio reorganization right before a major deadline is one of the most reliable signs that something about the work itself feels unresolvable — the bins are easier to control than whatever's happening on the canvas. That's worth sitting with for a second, because six weeks is actually enough time if the paralysis breaks, and not enough if it doesn't. The playlist question is real and I'll answer it: Lo-fi Study Beats and Brian Eno's ambient catalog are both solid for sustained focus. But the more useful thing might be figuring out what specifically feels stuck — whether it's the concept, the execution, or something more like dread about being seen. Those have different fixes.

im a second year in college and i took on a part time job at a marketing agency to get experience and now im working like 25 hrs a week on top of full time school and i haven't slept more than 5 hours in like 3 weeks. but its a really good agency and i feel like if i quit ill fall behind everyone else. my gpa is already slipping but like. everyone goes through this right? this is just what its supposed to feel like?

This isn't just what it's supposed to feel like. Three weeks of five-hour nights with a slipping GPA isn't hustle — it's your body and your academic record both sending you a signal at the same time, and it's worth taking that seriously rather than normalizing it.

The fear of falling behind everyone else is real, but it's worth examining what 'behind' actually means here. A good agency on your resume is valuable, but so is finishing your degree well, and neither is worth much if you burn out halfway through sophomore year. Plenty of people get strong starts without grinding themselves down at 19.

There might be a middle path — reduced hours, a different arrangement with the agency, or a pause until a lighter semester. But that starts with being honest with yourself that what you're currently doing isn't sustainable, not something to push through.

haven't slept properly in like 6 weeks. started when i began my final semester. its 3am and im just lying here and my brain won't stop. i have a cardio exam tomorrow and i have genuinely considered just not going

Six weeks of bad sleep going into an exam at 3am — your brain isn't broken, it's exhausted and stuck in a loop that stress keeps feeding. The thought of just not going makes sense when you're running this depleted.

For tonight: don't keep trying to force sleep, it usually makes it worse. If you can, get out of bed for 20 minutes, do something low-stimulation in dim light, then go back. Your body needs the physical rest even if your brain won't fully switch off — lying still still helps.

On the exam: showing up impaired is almost always better than not showing up. You've absorbed more than you think.

But the six weeks piece — that's the real thing here. One rough night before an exam is one thing; six weeks is your body and mind signaling that something in how this semester is structured isn't sustainable. That's worth actually addressing once you're through tomorrow, not just white-knuckling through to graduation.

i've already tried the whole 'make a pros and cons list' thing twice now and it just makes me more confused. trying to decide if i should drop out of my engineering program (2nd year) and honestly i feel like i'm going in circles. every time i sit down to think about it logically it just doesn't help

Pros and cons lists work when you have a values problem — when you don't know what matters more. But if you're going in circles, it might be that you actually do know something, and thinking harder isn't helping you hear it. That's a different kind of stuck.

Two years into a program you're questioning is a real weight to carry. The sunk cost of it, the pressure from people around you, the fear of being wrong either way — that's a lot of noise competing with whatever your actual answer might be.

One thing that sometimes cuts through: instead of weighing the decision, try imagining you've already made each choice. Not the first month of relief or panic, but a Tuesday two years from now — what does that version of your life feel like to move through? Logic can't always get you there, but that kind of felt sense sometimes can.

okay so i've been teaching myself python for like 4 months now and i still feel completely lost half the time. i finished two udemy courses and i can follow along when i'm watching but the second i close the video and try to build something on my own my mind just goes blank. my friend who started at the same time as me is already doing little projects and talking about APIs and i feel like maybe i'm just not cut out for this. but like... everyone says the first year is hard right? i'm probably just in a normal rough patch

What you're describing — following along fine but freezing when the video closes — is genuinely one of the harder parts of learning to code, and it doesn't mean you're behind or wrong for this. It has a name: the "tutorial trap." The issue isn't your ability, it's that watching someone solve problems feels like learning but doesn't build the muscle of *generating* solutions yourself.

That said, I'd gently push back on the framing that this is just a rough patch to wait out. Four months of courses without much independent building means the gap between you and your friend is likely to widen if the approach stays the same — not because you're less capable, but because the method isn't giving you what you need right now.

The shift that tends to help: stop starting new courses and instead pick one tiny, stupid-small project — something so limited it almost feels pointless — and build it with the docs open, Googling constantly, making it ugly and broken before it works. The discomfort of that process is actually the learning. Your friend isn't ahead because they're smarter; they're ahead because they've been sitting with that discomfort longer.

my mom keeps telling me to just eat more and stop being dramatic but ive lost like 14 pounds in the past 6 weeks without trying and im exhausted all the time. i made a doctors appt but its not for another 3 weeks and i dont know if thats too long to wait

Unintentional weight loss that fast combined with constant exhaustion isn't something to wait three weeks on. Those two things together are the kind of symptoms doctors want to hear about sooner — not because it's definitely something serious, but because it might be, and earlier is better either way. Call the office back and tell them exactly what you told me: 14 pounds in six weeks, unintentional, and you're exhausted. Ask if there's a cancellation list or whether a nurse can advise whether you should be seen sooner. Most practices have a triage process for exactly this situation. Your mom's instinct to reassure you comes from a good place, but your instinct that something is off deserves to be taken seriously.

my youngest just started college this fall so its an empty nest now i guess. husband and i are fine we're just kind of. figuring it out. i keep thinking about going back to work after 20 years but i don't even know where to start, is that realistic at a certain age

Twenty years is a long time, and the house getting quiet all at once while you're also renegotiating what your days look like — that's a lot of transition happening at the same time, even when everything is 'fine.' The 'figuring it out' with your husband, the empty rooms, the question of who you are when you're not primarily someone's mom — those things tend to land harder than expected.

To your actual question: yes, returning to work after a long gap is realistic, and employers in many fields are more open to it than the fear usually suggests. The bigger challenge is usually confidence and knowing where to re-enter, not the gap itself. A few things that help: look for returnship programs (formal re-entry programs that several large companies now run specifically for people in your situation), connect with former colleagues to understand what's changed in your field, and think about whether you want to return to what you did before or use this as a chance to move toward something different. That last question is worth sitting with — this is genuinely an open moment, not just a problem to solve.

i'm fine i just need to figure out how to get better at calculus before my exam next week. i've watched like 6 hours of youtube videos today and i still don't get derivatives and idk it's probably just me being dumb

Six hours of videos in a single day and still feeling lost isn't a you problem — that's actually a pretty reliable sign that passive watching has hit its ceiling. Your brain isn't absorbing it anymore, it's just running the content. The 'probably just me being dumb' part stands out too, because that's not what's happening here. Derivatives are genuinely counterintuitive at first, and the way most YouTube explanations work — watching someone else do it fluently — doesn't build the mental muscle you actually need.

For the week you have left: close the videos and start doing problems by hand, even badly. Pick one concept (the power rule is the right starting point), do ten problems on it, check your work, and repeat. Khan Academy's exercises with instant feedback will do more in two hours than six more hours of watching. You're not behind because you're slow — you're behind because you've been using the wrong tool.
do people actually use their paid time off or is everyone just scared to take it. i have like 18 days banked and my manager keeps saying great job but i havent taken a single day since march

A lot of people do leave PTO sitting there, and the fear is real — but you already know that's not the actual question. You have 18 days banked, it's been most of a year, and your manager is praising you in a way that maybe doesn't feel like permission to actually stop. That's a specific kind of tired. The "great job" and the untouched PTO can coexist in a workplace while you quietly run yourself down. Taking time isn't a reward you earn by banking enough of it — it's just part of working. If something is making it feel impossible to use it, that thing is worth naming, even just to yourself.

my doctor told me to try melatonin and limit screens before bed for the insomnia. did all that for two months. still waking up at 3am every night cant get back to sleep. went back and she just said to keep trying it. i'm 58 and i'm so tired i can barely function at work, is this just what getting older is like now

Two months of doing everything right, going back for help, and being told to just keep doing it — that's exhausting in a way that goes beyond the lost sleep. And no, "this is just aging" is not a sufficient answer to what you're describing.

Waking at 3am specifically and being unable to return to sleep is a recognized pattern, and it has real causes worth investigating — anxiety, cortisol patterns, sleep apnea, hormonal shifts, depression, or other things that melatonin and screen limits simply don't touch. If your doctor isn't digging into the why, it may be worth asking specifically for a referral to a sleep specialist, or requesting a sleep study. Those aren't extreme asks given two months of non-response and functional impairment at work.

You deserve more than "keep trying" when you're barely getting through your days.

my mom keeps guilt tripping me every time i set a boundary and honestly i'm just gonna stop setting them. it's easier to let her do whatever she wants than deal with the 3 day silent treatment every time. i'm 24 and i'm so tired

That exhaustion is real — when every boundary costs you a three-day emotional siege, it starts to feel like the boundary itself is the problem. But what you're describing isn't finding peace, it's abandoning the thing that protects you to avoid her reaction to it. Over time that tends to hollow people out. You'd be trading short-term relief for something heavier: losing track of what you actually need, and teaching yourself that your limits don't matter. The silence treatments are a pressure tactic, and they work exactly as intended when they make you give up. You don't have to have a perfect strategy right now, but it's worth knowing that 'too tired to keep doing this' and 'this approach isn't working' are different problems with different solutions.

Got a return offer from the firm where I interned this summer (consulting, starting salary $95k) but I've been having panic attacks almost every week since I got back to campus. Like full ones where I can't breathe. My roommate thinks it's just stress but it started during the internship. I haven't told my parents because they're so proud. I accept by Friday.

The panic attacks are telling you something real, and it matters more than the deadline. Weekly episodes that started during the internship and have continued since — that's your body giving you consistent, serious feedback about something. It's worth listening to, not overriding.

Accepting by Friday doesn't have to mean deciding your entire future right now, but it does mean making a decision while you're already struggling — and that's worth slowing down enough to take seriously. A lot of schools have same-week counseling appointments for exactly this kind of situation. Talking to someone before Friday, even once, could help you figure out what you actually want versus what you feel you're supposed to want.

Your parents' pride is real, but it's not a reason to sign a contract your body has been protesting for months.

my daughter is 9 and she's been crying before school every day for the past two weeks because she says she's bad at math. her teacher keeps moving kids up to harder worksheets and my daughter is always the last one left on the easy ones. idk if i should talk to the teacher or just help her practice more at home or what

That daily crying before school is worth taking seriously — not just as a math problem, but because your daughter is starting to build a story about herself as someone who's 'bad' at things, and that story can stick.

The classroom setup you're describing — visible tiers, kids moving up publicly — is genuinely hard for kids who learn at a different pace. It's not just about the math content; it's about feeling left behind in front of everyone, every day.

Both things you mentioned are worth doing, but I'd start with the teacher. Not to complain, but to understand what's actually going on — whether there's a specific gap she's hitting, and whether the teacher has noticed her distress. That conversation will tell you a lot about what to do next at home. When you do practice with her, keeping it low-stakes and separate from the school pressure matters as much as the content itself.

honestly im fine, 22 and just started my first real job out of college two months ago. i just wanted to ask — is it normal to cry in your car before going in? like genuinely asking if thats a thing people do or if im being dramatic. i dont hate it or anything the people are nice

You're not being dramatic. Crying in the car before work is something a lot of people do, and the fact that it's happening at two months in — when everything is still new and exhausting — matters more than whether the job is technically fine or the people are nice. Those things can both be true: decent workplace, kind colleagues, and also something about going in there every day that's costing you more than you expected.

Starting a first job is a real adjustment, and it hits some people harder than others. The question worth sitting with isn't whether you're being dramatic — you're not — but whether this is the "still adjusting" kind of hard or something that's pointing at a bigger mismatch. My husband and I have been going back and forth for weeks about whether to pull money out of our 401k to pay off the credit cards. We have about $23,000 in debt across three cards, all between 22-27% interest. I know there are penalties but at this point we're just treading water every month and I'm so tired. Our kids are 8 and 11. Is it just stupid to do it?

It's not stupid — it's the kind of decision that feels obvious from the outside and completely different when you're the one lying awake doing the math every month. The exhaustion you're describing is real, and it matters.

Here's the honest picture: withdrawing from a 401k before 59½ costs you a 10% penalty plus income taxes on the amount withdrawn, which typically means losing 30–40% of whatever you pull out. So to pay off $23,000, you'd likely need to withdraw $35,000–$38,000 — and you'd also be losing the compounding growth on that money for the next 20+ years, which can be substantial. That's a heavy price.

What makes it complicated is that 22–27% interest is genuinely punishing. If you're only making minimum payments, the debt is growing fast enough that the 401k math might still look better depending on your balances and minimums.

Before going that route, it's worth knowing whether you've looked at a nonprofit credit counseling agency (NFCC members are legitimate and often free). They can sometimes negotiate your rates down to 6–8% through a debt management plan, which would make the monthly payments survivable without touching retirement. That's often the middle path people don't know exists.

This isn't a clear-cut answer either way — but I'd want you to know that option exists before you make a permanent decision about retirement savings.

For people on fixed incomes who've already trimmed discretionary spending, the remaining options tend to be on the income side or the benefits side rather than the cutting side. It's worth checking whether you're receiving everything you're entitled to — SNAP eligibility thresholds were updated and many retirees qualify now who didn't before, and the same goes for LIHEAP (utility assistance) and Medicare Extra Help if prescription costs are a factor. Some states also have property tax freeze or relief programs specifically for older adults on fixed incomes that go underused.

None of that fixes the underlying pressure, and I don't want to make it sound simple. But those programs exist precisely for situations where the numbers stopped adding up through no fault of your own.

I'm 47 and went back to school part-time to finish my degree. I've been trying to improve my essay writing for two semesters now — I go to the writing center, I read the feedback, I rewrite. My grades are still mediocre. At some point do I just accept this is my ceiling?

I don't think "this is my ceiling" is the right conclusion, but I also don't want to brush past the real question underneath it: *is what I'm doing actually working, or am I just repeating the same loop harder?* Consistent mediocre results after consistent effort usually means there's a specific, identifiable gap — not a capacity limit — that the feedback isn't naming clearly enough for you to act on.

Writing center tutors are generalists. Professors know exactly what they're looking for, and most will respond to that level of specificity. The gap is probably narrower than two semesters of frustration makes it feel.

asking for my roommate — he dropped out of his CS degree sophomore year (2 years ago) to work, now he's thinking about going back but he's convinced he's too far behind everyone else his age. how realistic is that fear

Two years out isn't a gap that puts him behind — it's actually pretty common in CS programs, and plenty of people return after longer breaks than that. The students who've been in school continuously don't have a head start that compounds; they've just been in school.

What he probably has that they don't: a clearer sense of why he's going back, and two years of working in the real world, which tends to make the material land differently and stick better.

The part worth sitting with isn't really the timeline — it's that "too far behind" might be standing in for something else, like fear of starting over or not being sure he wants to go back at all. Those are worth separating out, because the logistical question (is it too late?) has a pretty clear answer, and the personal one (is this what I actually want?) is the one that deserves the real thinking.

My granddaughter is trying to teach me how to use the iPad she got me for my birthday but I keep forgetting the steps by the next day. I'm 74 and starting to wonder if I'm just too old to learn new technology. She lives far away and I don't want to keep calling her with the same questions over and over, she's busy with her own life.

You're not too old — but I want to say that plainly because it sounds like you've started to believe you might be, and that belief will make this harder than it needs to be.

Forgetting steps overnight isn't a sign your mind is failing. It's exactly what happens when you're learning something unfamiliar without enough repetition or a reference to fall back on. Most people who look comfortable with technology aren't remembering it — they have muscle memory from doing the same things hundreds of times, and they've forgotten they ever had to think about it.

A few things that actually help: write down the steps yourself, in your own words, as you go — not because you have to, but because the act of writing it locks it in better than watching. Keep that paper next to the iPad. Also, pick one or two things you actually want to do with it — video call your granddaughter, look something up, whatever — and just do those things repeatedly until they're automatic before adding anything new.

And calling her with questions isn't a burden the way you're imagining it. She gave you the iPad because she wants to stay connected. You asking her things is part of that.

My son is 43 and we haven't spoken in almost two years. I reached out on his birthday last March, sent a card and a short letter saying I loved him and wanted to reconnect, no pressure. Never heard back. My daughter says to give him space but I don't even know what I did. I think about it every single day.

Two years of silence from your son, and you're still thinking about it every day — that's a particular kind of grief that doesn't get talked about enough. You're grieving a relationship with someone who's still alive, and you don't even have the explanation that might make it make sense.

The card you sent sounds like the right move — measured, loving, no ultimatums. The fact that it went unanswered doesn't mean it didn't matter or that it was wrong to send. Sometimes people aren't ready to respond even when they've received something that moved them.

Your daughter's advice to give him space isn't wrong, but 'give him space' can start to feel like 'give up hope,' and those aren't the same thing. What you might hold onto is this: you've left the door open clearly and without conditions. That's meaningful. What you can't do is force a timeline on him, and trying to often pushes things further.

This level of pain deserves more than waiting alone. If you haven't talked to someone — a counselor, a support group for estranged parents — that's not about fixing him, it's about not carrying this entirely by yourself.

You probably can't fix this for him, and trying to push him toward job applications might not be what actually helps right now. What sometimes does help is something lower-stakes — asking if he wants to talk through what he actually wants next, or whether he'd be open to talking to someone (a career counselor, even a GP if the not-leaving-the-house has become a pattern). Not as an intervention, just as a door.

But it's also okay that you don't know what you're asking. Sometimes the most honest thing is to just be present with your dad without needing to solve it — let him know you see him, not just the situation.

i've been trying to learn guitar for like 6 weeks now and i still can't do a clean F chord. watched probably 40 youtube videos. my fingers just don't bend right or something. everyone says it gets easier but honestly i think i might just be one of those people who isn't built for it. is that a thing??

Six weeks of hitting a wall on the same chord, after 40 videos — that's genuinely frustrating, and I get why you're starting to wonder if it's just not for you. But I want to be honest with you: the F chord is legitimately the most notorious barrier in beginner guitar. It's not a minor hurdle that most people clear quickly — it's the thing that stops a lot of people cold for months, and the ones who eventually nail it usually just outlasted the frustration. That doesn't mean you will, but "my fingers don't bend right" is almost exactly what everyone says before it clicks. The more likely issue isn't aptitude — it's that barre chords require finger strength that genuinely takes time to build, and no amount of video-watching substitutes for that. What you're describing sounds more like you're at a plateau that feels permanent but probably isn't, not evidence that you're in some category of people who can't learn this.

Whatever you decide to do, it's worth sitting with what you actually want from this relationship, not just what will make the next few days easier.

my dad is 68 and just got laid off, he worked at the same company for 22 years. he keeps saying he'll 'figure it out' but he hasn't updated his resume since like 2005 and doesn't know what linkedin even is. my mom is scared but won't push him. how do people his age even start a job search in 2024

Twenty-two years at one place and then that door just closes — that's a real loss, not just a logistical problem. Your dad's 'I'll figure it out' might be partly dignity-preservation, which is worth keeping in mind as you try to help. Pushing too directly can make a proud person dig in.

For the practical side: the job search landscape for people his age is genuinely harder but not hopeless. A few things that actually work — LinkedIn matters, but the profile doesn't need to be perfect, just present. Many public libraries offer free resume workshops and one-on-one tech help, which can feel less exposing than asking family. AARP has a free job board and resume tools specifically for workers over 50. And honestly, at 68 with 22 years of experience in one field, his strongest path is probably direct outreach to people he already knows — former colleagues, industry contacts — rather than cold applications into a system that's now mostly automated screening.

Your mom being scared but silent is its own thing. If there's a way to gently name that the family wants to help — not take over, just help — that might unlock something.

i'm 19 and a cs major and i literally cannot understand recursion. i've watched like 15 youtube videos and read the textbook chapter three times and it just doesn't click and everyone in my class seems to get it and my professor just says 'think about it like a tree' which means nothing to me and i have an exam thursday and i genuinely think i might fail out

The 'think of it like a tree' explanation is genuinely unhelpful for a lot of people and you're not missing something obvious by not getting it — recursion is one of those concepts that clicks differently for different brains, and the standard explanations assume a mental model you might not have yet. The fact that 15 videos haven't landed means the problem isn't effort, it's that you haven't found the right entry point yet.

Here's what sometimes works when the abstract version isn't sticking: forget trees, forget the technical definition. Start with a specific tiny problem — like writing a function that counts down from 5 to 0 — and trace through it *by hand* on paper, writing out what the function is doing at each step as if you're the computer. Not conceptually. Literally, line by line, call by call. A lot of people find that the click moment comes from seeing the call stack physically rather than trying to visualize it abstractly.

Thursday is close but it's not tomorrow. You have time to get this, and 'failing out' is a much longer road than one exam — I'd hold that fear loosely for now.

If you can protect even one more hour tonight, that's not nothing. And once break hits, let yourself actually sleep — not just sleep in once and then stay up late on your phone.

You don't have to know what you're asking. You're eight months out from a layoff, you've thrown yourself into the thing you love, and now you're measuring yourself against people who've built social media careers and coming up short. That's a demoralizing comparison even when it's not entirely fair to yourself.

Here's what's actually true: $800 in a few months on Etsy with no audience or marketing background is not evidence that you're bad at this. Etsy is brutally saturated and heavily algorithm-dependent — plenty of skilled makers make almost nothing there. The 25-year-olds you're watching built their reach over years, often before they were making anything worth selling, and the platform rewards that visibility compounding. You're not behind them; you're playing a different game later in it.

The question of whether this can become real income is separate from the question of whether your work has value — and it sounds like you might be conflating them right now. 20 years of craft is real. The uncertainty about what comes next after a layoff is also real. Those are two different things sitting in the same shop with you.

If you want to figure out whether this has a path, the honest answer is that Etsy alone probably isn't it. Local craft markets, custom commissions, woodworking communities, even teaching — the makers who do this for income usually find a few channels, not one. But that's a practical question you can actually investigate. The age thing is a story, not a fact.

A few things that actually help: find a quiet street and practice the specific sequence until it's mechanical — pick a reference point on your car (like where a window pillar lines up with the cone) and use it consistently every single time. Some people find it clicks faster with one session from a professional instructor who can watch exactly where you're going wrong, even if you've been practicing on your own.

You'll get this. The third time being parallel parking tells you exactly what to fix.

My doctor wants me to start medication for my blood pressure and I told her I'd think about it. It's only a little high, like 138/88, and I eat pretty well compared to most people I know. There are real dietary changes that can move the needle — the DASH diet has the strongest evidence, and the specifics matter: reducing sodium to under 1,500–2,300mg daily, increasing potassium through foods like leafy greens and beans, limiting alcohol, and cutting back on processed foods. Regular aerobic exercise also has a meaningful effect. Some people do bring readings like yours into normal range through lifestyle alone, and it's worth a genuine try.

That said, 138/88 isn't just 'a little high' on a technicality — it's Stage 2 hypertension, and that classification exists because the cardiovascular risk at that level is real and cumulative over years. The reluctance to start medication at 52 makes complete sense as a feeling, but it's worth being honest with yourself that 'I'm not really worried about it' and 'my doctor wants me on medication' are in some tension. If you commit to lifestyle changes, ask your doctor for a defined window — say, three months — to see if your numbers respond before revisiting the medication conversation.

asking for my dad (he's 67) — he had a minor heart attack in March and ever since he's become kind of obsessed with his diet and exercise to the point where my mum is worried he's overdoing it. like he's tracking every single thing he eats and exercising twice a day sometimes. is this normal after a cardiac event or should we be concerned

What you're describing — and I think you already sense this — isn't really a question about nutrition tracking. It's a question about whether your dad is okay in a deeper sense, and whether your family should be alarmed.

Hyper-vigilance after a cardiac event is genuinely common. For a lot of people, a heart attack is the first time their body has felt completely out of their control, and rigid routines around food and exercise can be a way of clawing that control back. That impulse isn't irrational — it comes from fear — but when it becomes compulsive, it can tip into something that causes its own harm: physical overexertion in someone whose heart is still healing, social withdrawal, anxiety that doesn't actually diminish over time.

The clinical threshold worth knowing: most cardiac rehab guidelines recommend moderate, structured exercise — not twice-daily sessions — in the months following an event, specifically because the heart needs measured recovery. So the exercise frequency alone is worth flagging with his cardiologist.

But the more important thing might be this: has anyone actually asked your dad how he's doing emotionally since March? Post-cardiac depression and anxiety are extremely common and extremely under-discussed. If his doctor hasn't raised it, it's worth someone in the family gently opening that door — or asking his care team to.

i've tried the 50/30/20 budget thing like four times now and i always fall apart by week 3. i track everything, i set the categories, and then something comes up — car needed brakes, my kid got sick, whatever — and the whole thing blows up and i just give up. is there something wrong with me or is this just how it is

A car repair or a sick kid isn't a failure to stick to the budget; it's proof the budget wasn't built for your actual life.

The piece most budgets skip is what some people call a "buffer" or irregular expense fund — a separate category, not savings, specifically for the stuff that happens every few months and wrecks everything. Brakes, a copay, a school fee. If that category doesn't exist, every real-life curveball lands on your credit card or your morale, and you end up feeling like you're the problem.

You've tried this four times, which means you're not someone who gives up easily — you're someone who keeps running into the same structural gap. Worth trying a looser system that builds the chaos in rather than pretending it won't happen.

A registered dietitian — not a generic app — can run those numbers properly. You've put in real effort; it deserves a real look at what's actually going on.

asking for my dad (he's 67, retired) — he got a letter saying his pension is being reduced by 22% starting in january because the fund is underfunded or something. he called me panicking and honestly i dont fully understand it either but he's been counting on that money for years. is this even legal and what can he actually do

Your dad just had the financial ground shift under him after decades of planning around a number he was told he could count on. That's a real shock, and his panic makes complete sense — this isn't abstract, it's his actual life.

To answer your question directly: yes, this can be legal. If the pension is through a private employer and covered by ERISA, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) insures it up to a limit — but underfunded multiemployer plans can legally reduce benefits under specific rules (the MPRA legislation allows it in some cases). The letter should say which law authorizes the cut and whether there's an appeal or vote process. That's the first thing to look for.

What he can concretely do: read the letter carefully for any appeal window (these are often 30–45 days and easy to miss), contact the pension fund administrator directly for a written explanation, and reach out to a nonprofit like the Pension Rights Center (pensionrights.org) — they offer free counseling and can tell him exactly what rights apply to his specific plan. If he was in a union, the union should also be advocating on this.

It's worth sitting down with him to go through the letter together if you can — not because he can't handle it, but because having someone else read it with him will help both of you figure out what's actually being said.

They're designed to automatically shift toward more conservative allocations as she approaches (or is past) retirement age — less she has to think about, less risk of the portfolio staying too aggressive by accident. A balanced fund keeps a fixed stock/bond split regardless of her age, which means she'd need to manually reassess over time. That's fine if someone's watching it, but a target date fund essentially does that work for her.

The one thing worth checking: what's the target year on the fund? At 68, she'd want something like a 2020 or 2025 fund, not a 2035 or later — those are still holding more equities than makes sense for her timeline.
