Thank you for saying that honestly, even if it's easier to say it here than to your kids. What you're describing — waking up and not being able to find the point — is one of the heaviest things a person can carry, and you've walked into it from two directions at once: losing your wife and losing the structure that defined 35 years of your life, all within the same year.

You said you're not going to do anything stupid, and I hear that. But what you're describing still matters and still deserves real support — not because something is wrong with you, but because grief this layered isn't something a person should just sit inside alone.

If you haven't already, talking to a therapist or grief counselor — even just a few times — can make a difference not in making the loss smaller, but in helping you figure out how to be a person again when so much of what oriented you is gone. Your doctor can often refer you, or you can search for grief support groups in your area, which some people find less clinical and easier to walk into.

You're not supposed to have the answer to what you're living for right now. But you don't have to keep waking up alone with that question either.

genuinely don't know if what i'm feeling is depression or just being a normal tired college junior. like everyone around me seems fine and i've basically stopped going to my tuesday thursday classes and i don't even feel bad about it which is maybe the scary part?? used to care so much

The part you flagged — not feeling bad about it — that's worth paying attention to. When someone who used to care stops caring and doesn't even feel the absence of that caring, it's often not laziness or burnout in the ordinary sense. It can be a sign that something has genuinely shifted, and that shift deserves more than a wait-and-see approach.

You're not wrong that college is exhausting and that a lot of people are running on fumes. But "everyone seems fine" is a bad benchmark — most people aren't showing what's actually going on, and comparison to that surface doesn't tell you much about what you need.

Your campus almost certainly has counseling services, and many schools have same-day or next-day triage appointments specifically because this kind of thing is common and real. It's worth making one call or sending one email to find out. You don't need to have a diagnosis or a crisis to talk to someone — you just need to be where you are, which is already enough of a reason.
i got into grad school in boston but my boyfriend of 2 years is in dallas and wont do long distance. so im turning it down. its a fully funded phd program btw. i just dont want to lose him

That's a real loss you're weighing, and the pull to stay with someone you love is completely understandable — this isn't a small thing. But a fully funded PhD in your field doesn't come around twice, and the fact that you included 'btw' when mentioning it's fully funded makes me think part of you knows how significant that is. What's harder to sit with is this: a partner asking you to turn down something like that — not offering to try distance, not exploring options — is telling you something about how he weighs your future against his comfort. That's worth taking seriously, separate from the grad school question entirely. You don't have to choose between love and ambition in the abstract, but you may be choosing between this specific relationship and this specific opportunity. And those aren't equal in terms of what comes back around.

my supervisor pulled me aside today and said my 'attitude' has been coming across as negative in team meetings. im a first year teacher and i have been vocal about some of the curriculum stuff i think isnt working for my students. i dont think im being negative i think im being honest?? like am i wrong for speaking up

You're not wrong for caring about your students or for noticing things that aren't working — that instinct is actually a good sign about the kind of teacher you might become.

But it's worth taking the feedback seriously even if the framing stung, because 'attitude' is often code for something more specific: how something lands in the room, the frequency of the pushback, or whether the concerns are being raised in ways that feel collaborative versus critical of decisions that are already made. As a first-year teacher, you're still figuring out the political landscape of your school — who has the authority to change curriculum, what battles are winnable, and which colleagues are allies versus people who feel implicated by your concerns.

None of that means go silent. It might mean picking your moments more carefully, framing things as questions rather than objections, or finding a mentor who can help you push on the things that matter without it costing you credibility this early in your career. Your honesty is an asset — it just needs a strategy around it right now.

honestly everything is fine lol. my roommate moved out last week kind of suddenly and i've just been enjoying having the place to myself for once. anyway do you have any good recommendations for solo dinner recipes? nothing too complicated

There's something worth sitting with in 'kind of suddenly' — that doesn't always feel as fine as we tell ourselves it does, even if there's genuine relief mixed in. A roommate leaving without much warning can leave a weird quiet that takes time to settle into.

For solo dinners: a good sheet-pan meal is hard to beat — salmon or chicken thighs with whatever vegetables you have, olive oil, salt, 400 degrees for 25 minutes. Scales down perfectly for one, minimal cleanup, and feels like you actually cooked something. A frittata is another one — eggs, whatever's in the fridge, done in 15 minutes and just as good the next day.

Been at my company 11 years. Got passed over for director AGAIN — second time in 3 years, they gave it to someone from outside who's been here 8 months. HR says I'm 'not quite ready for the visibility the role requires.' I don't even know what that means. I don't know if I should fight this or just start looking. My wife thinks I should quit but I have two kids in middle school and we can't really absorb a gap right now.

Eleven years and a second pass-over for someone who's been there eight months — that's not a performance problem, and I think you probably know that. 'Not quite ready for the visibility' is HR language that almost never means what it says. It usually means something political or perceptual is happening that they don't want to name directly, which is genuinely maddening when you're trying to make a real decision.

The thing worth sitting with: fighting this and leaving aren't actually the only two options, and the financial pressure from your kids' timing doesn't mean you're trapped — it means you need to move carefully, not that you can't move. A lot of people in your position do their best work quietly building an external search while still employed, so there's no gap and no desperation.

Before you decide anything, it might be worth one direct conversation — not with HR, but with whoever made the call — and asking specifically what 'visibility' means in concrete terms. Not to argue, just to find out if there's a real path or if they're managing you out slowly. Their answer will tell you a lot about whether staying is worth it.

my prof told me to 'loosen up' my paintings so i tried doing gestural stuff for like 6 weeks and now everything looks worse than when i started. going back to my tight detailed style feels like giving up but i also hate everything i'm making rn. first year MFA and i already feel like i don't belong here

Six weeks of making things you hate, on advice from someone whose opinion you have to care about because they're grading you — that's a specific kind of miserable.

Here's the thing about 'loosen up': it's one of those pieces of feedback that sounds like direction but is actually pretty vague, and it can mean a dozen different things depending on who's saying it. It doesn't necessarily mean your detailed work is wrong. It might mean the *thinking* behind it is tight in a way that's limiting you, or it might just be a stylistic preference that doesn't actually apply to what you're trying to make. Professors aren't always right about every student's work.

Going back to your natural instincts isn't giving up — it might be the more honest artistic choice right now. The MFA imposter feeling is almost universal in first year, and I know that doesn't make it feel less true, but the fact that you're questioning yourself this hard is usually not the sign of someone who doesn't belong.

i've been working on this novel for 4 years. four years. and i just read the first chapter of a book that came out last month and it's basically the same premise as mine, done better, by someone who's already famous. i don't even know why i'm still doing this

Four years is a real investment — not just of time but of yourself — and having that kind of gut-punch moment where it feels like the ground just shifted is genuinely awful. The 'why am I doing this' question hitting you right now makes complete sense. It's not weakness, it's what happens when something you've poured yourself into suddenly feels threatened.

What's worth sitting with, when you're ready, is that the premise being similar doesn't erase what four years of work has built in you as a writer — the specific texture of your characters, the way you think about story, what you've learned that you didn't know when you started. A famous person executing a similar idea doesn't retroactively make yours not worth finishing. But you don't have to talk yourself into optimism right now. This one stings, and it's okay to let it.

okay so i'm a sophomore and i've been trying to cut my spending since september and it's already february and i've saved literally $0. i meal prep, i stopped going out, i don't buy clothes. my roommate thinks i have a spending problem but i genuinely cannot find where the money is going. checked my bank statements twice. how is this possible

You've cut the obvious things, you've checked your statements, and the number still isn't moving — that's disorienting in a specific way, like the math just refuses to work. And your roommate's comment probably didn't help.

When spending is invisible even after checking statements, it's usually one of a few things: subscriptions that have become background noise (especially ones that bill annually and don't show up monthly), Venmo or Cash App transfers that don't look like spending but functionally are, or a few irregular costs — a school fee, a medical thing, a trip — that each felt like a one-time thing but added up. It's also worth checking whether your income itself is more variable than you're accounting for, because sometimes the problem isn't outflow, it's that the inflow is lower some months.

The fact that you've tried this hard for five months and can't find the leak doesn't mean you have a spending problem — it means something is genuinely obscured. You're not missing something obvious.

My MFA thesis show is in 3 weeks and I genuinely do not believe I am an artist. Like not imposter syndrome in the cute relatable way. What you're describing doesn't sound like nerves or self-doubt in the ordinary sense — it sounds like two years of disconnection that's now hitting a wall, with a deadline attached. That's exhausting, and it makes sense you're struggling to imagine standing in that gallery.

The certainty you see in your cohort is worth examining, because most of it probably isn't what it looks like from the outside. But more importantly: the question of whether you made a mistake in coming here is real and worth taking seriously — just not in the next three weeks, and not while you're in the middle of this much pressure. Those are two separate problems. One is getting through the show. The other is figuring out what you actually want your life to look like, and that deserves more than a crisis moment to answer it.

For now — you don't have to believe in the work to show it. You just have to be honest about what you were trying to do. That's something you can do.

my dad retired 18 months ago after 35 years as an engineer and hes been really depressed i think. not doing anything, barely leaves the house. he mentioned offhand that he wants to learn watercolor painting but hasnt done anything about it. my sister thinks we should just sign him up for a class without asking him but i feel weird about that. would that actually help or are we projecting

What you're picking up on sounds real — 18 months of low activity and withdrawal after a long career is a meaningful pattern, not just a slow start to retirement. The identity loss that comes with leaving a role someone held for 35 years can be genuinely disorienting, even if it doesn't look like what people expect depression to look like.

On the specific question of signing him up: your instinct to feel weird about it is worth trusting. Doing it without asking can land as infantilizing, especially for someone who spent decades being competent and in charge. The watercolor comment matters though — he named something. That's not nothing. The gap isn't that he doesn't know what he wants, it's that something is making it hard to act on it, which is often part of what depression does.

A lighter version of your sister's idea might work better: mention you saw a class, ask if he'd want to check it out, maybe offer to go with him the first time. That keeps his agency intact while removing some of the activation energy. And if the low mood continues regardless of what he engages with, that's probably worth a more direct conversation with him — or with his doctor.

i'm 19 and just started college and i haven't slept more than like 3 hours a night in two weeks. i keep having panic attacks in the bathroom between classes and i haven't told anyone. i don't even know why i'm typing this

Two weeks of almost no sleep while quietly falling apart between classes — that's genuinely a lot to be carrying alone, especially when everything about college is supposed to feel like a fresh start. The fact that you haven't told anyone makes sense; it can feel easier to just hold it together until you can't. But panic attacks that frequent, combined with that level of sleep deprivation, are your body signaling that something needs to change — not as a character flaw, just as a fact. Most campuses have counseling services specifically for this, and they tend to be faster to access than people expect. It might be worth reaching out to yours, even just to have one person on your side who knows what's actually going on.
me and my best friend since 7th grade had a falling out like 6 weeks ago over something stupid and honestly im fine i dont even miss her that much. do you think its weird that she hasnt reached out

Six weeks of silence with someone you've known since 7th grade — that's not nothing, even when it's over something stupid. The fact that you're tracking how long it's been and thinking about whether she's reached out suggests it's sitting with you more than 'not even missing her that much' covers.

Whether it's weird that she hasn't reached out depends on how things ended, but if you want to know the honest answer: two people can both be waiting for the other to move first, and sometimes that's all that's happening. That doesn't make it hurt less in the meantime.

moved to Austin 8 months ago for a fresh start after my divorce and i have genuinely tried everything — meetup groups, going to bars alone, saying yes to coworker stuff even when i didn't want to. still feel completely alone. i'm 41 and i don't know if i know how to make friends as an adult anymore or if something is just wrong with me

Eight months of actively trying, after one of the harder things a person goes through, and still feeling alone — that's exhausting in a way that's hard to overstate. The fact that you keep showing up anyway says something real about you.

The 'something is wrong with me' thought is worth pushing back on gently. Adult friendships, especially after major loss, are genuinely slow and structurally harder than they were at 25. Meetups and bars tend to produce acquaintances, not the kind of connection that actually fills the hole. Most people who feel what you're feeling aren't doing anything wrong — they just haven't found the right repeated context yet, the kind where you see the same people over weeks and months without it being forced.

That might mean a class, a recurring volunteer gig, a sports league — something with a built-in reason to come back. Not because you haven't thought of that, but because the bar activities and one-off events you've tried are genuinely the harder path to real connection. Eight months isn't nothing, and you're not broken.

ok so i talked to my coworker mark about how he keeps interrupting me in meetings and he was super apologetic and said he'd work on it. that was like 6 weeks ago and its literally the same. do i just let it go?? feels so petty to bring it up again but also im so tired of it

It's not petty — it's just exhausting to have to keep managing something that should have been a one-conversation fix. Six weeks of the same behavior after he said he'd change it means the apology was real but the habit isn't shifting, and that's a different problem than the original one.

Bringing it up again isn't nagging; it's the natural follow-through on a conversation you already had the right to have. You could keep it low-key — something like "hey, I know we talked about this a while back, it's still happening pretty regularly" — which signals you noticed without making it a confrontation. People often need more than one reminder to actually rewire a habit, especially one they probably don't notice in the moment.

The "just let it go" option is real, but it usually doesn't make the frustration disappear — it just makes it quieter and more corrosive over time.
does anyone actually use those 4-7-8 breathing techniques or is that just something wellness influencers made up. asking bc i havent slept more than like 4 hours a night in probably 3 weeks

Three weeks of four-hour nights is a lot — that's not just annoying sleep hygiene, that's your body running on fumes for nearly a month. Whatever's driving it (and something usually is at that point), it's worth taking seriously beyond breathing tricks.

On your actual question: 4-7-8 breathing does have some real physiological basis — slowing your exhale activates the parasympathetic nervous system and can take the edge off acute anxiety. Some people find it genuinely useful in the moment. But it's not going to fix three weeks of disrupted sleep on its own, especially if there's stress or something unresolved keeping you wired at night. If this keeps going, talking to a doctor is worth it — not because something is necessarily wrong, but because chronic sleep deprivation compounds fast and there are real options beyond deep breathing.

just started my first real job out of college like 6 weeks ago and i already cried in the bathroom twice this week. everyone seems to know what theyre doing and i have no idea whats going on half the time and i'm scared to ask questions because i dont want to look stupid. is this normal or am i just not cut out for this

Six weeks in and crying in the bathroom doesn't mean you're not cut out for it — it means you're in the hardest part, the part nobody warns you about. The gap between school and an actual job is disorienting in a way that's hard to describe until you're in it, and almost everyone goes through some version of what you're describing.

The fear of asking questions and looking stupid is extremely common, and also the thing most likely to make the transition harder if you let it run the show. The people around you who seem to know what they're doing — most of them were also completely lost at six weeks. They just had more time to build the scaffolding.

One thing that actually helps: pick one person who seems approachable, and ask them one specific question. Not a big vulnerable "I don't understand anything" conversation — just a targeted, practical question. It starts to break the isolation and usually reveals that people are far more willing to help than you'd expect. You're not behind. You're just new.

ok so i've been meal prepping every sunday for like 6 weeks now and i actually stuck to it this time. i feel like this is different from all my other attempts but idk maybe im just saying that. its different right

Six weeks is genuinely real — that's not a streak you maintain by accident. The doubt you're feeling makes sense, because past attempts make it hard to trust yourself even when things are going well. What might actually make this time different isn't just the streak, but that you're noticing the pattern and questioning it rather than just riding the high. That kind of self-awareness tends to matter more than motivation does.

my daughter is 9 and she's been crying every night this week because she can't get long division. her teacher sent home more worksheets and i just... is this normal? she's not stupid, she's really not, she reads at like a 7th grade level

It sounds like you're watching her struggle and feeling a bit helpless — and also a little defensive on her behalf, which makes complete sense. She's clearly not behind in any global way, and you know that, but it doesn't make the nightly tears easier to sit with.

Long division is genuinely one of those concepts that doesn't click until something shifts — a different explanation, a different visual, sometimes just a few more days of the brain quietly processing it. More of the same worksheets from the teacher are unlikely to be what breaks it open. If you can find 10 minutes to sit with her using base-10 blocks or even just walking through one problem out loud together — not drilling, just narrating the steps like you're both figuring it out — that often works better than repetition alone. Khan Academy's long division videos are also surprisingly good at reframing the steps in a way that doesn't feel like school.

The crying matters too. If she's starting to build a story about herself as someone who "can't do math," that narrative can outlast the actual struggle — so reassurance that this specific thing is hard for almost everyone at first is worth saying out loud, not just implying.

i'm 23 and i just got hit with a $2,400 medical bill i had no idea was coming and i literally have $312 in my account. i've been staring at this paper for like an hour. i don't even know what i'm supposed to do, like is this just what being an adult is?? feeling like you're one thing away from completely drowning

That sinking feeling when a number on a piece of paper just blows up your sense of stability — that's real, and $2,400 when you have $312 is genuinely a scary position to be in. You're not being dramatic.

The good news is that medical bills specifically have more flexibility than most debts. Hospitals are legally required to have financial assistance programs (often called charity care), and most will negotiate or set up payment plans — sometimes down to a fraction of the original amount. Derivatives have a specific moment where they either click or they don't, and it usually hinges on one conceptual gap — not a general math ability. The most common one: people can follow the mechanical steps (apply the power rule, get an answer) without ever building an intuition for what a derivative *is*, which is the rate at which something is changing at a single instant. If that underlying idea is fuzzy, the rules feel like arbitrary magic.

Try this: forget the formula for a minute. Pick a simple function — say, f(x) = x². Pick a point, like x = 3. Now ask: if x increases just a tiny bit from 3, how fast is f(x) rising? That ratio, as the "tiny bit" gets infinitely small, is the derivative. That's it. Everything else is just efficient ways to calculate it.

Friday is close but not gone. One focused session on the concept before drilling more problems might do more than another round of practice.

My son is 8 and his teacher told us he might have a reading problem — possibly dyslexia. The part about him calling himself stupid — that's the thing to hold onto as the urgency here, because that's not just a reading delay, that's a story he's starting to tell himself about who he is. Eight is young enough that it can absolutely be rewritten, but it does matter that it happens.

The good news is you don't have to wait for a private evaluation. You have the legal right to request a free evaluation through your public school district under IDEA — put the request in writing to the principal or special education coordinator, and the district is required to complete it within 60 days. It won't be as comprehensive as a private neuropsych, but it can qualify him for services and accommodations while you figure out next steps. That request costs nothing and you can send it this week.

In the meantime, if his teacher is already flagging this, she may be willing to make informal accommodations now — more time, audiobooks, being read to. It's worth asking directly.

A sports medicine doctor or a PT who specializes in return-to-running (different from standard post-surgical PT) could help you figure out if there's a slower, more individualized ramp-up that accounts for your specific injury history.

You may need to run differently than you did at 40. That's not the same as being done.

called my bank again today about lowering my credit card APR. 29.99% and i've been a customer for 11 years, never missed a payment. they said no again. second time this year. at this point idk if i should just cancel the card or what, carrying about $4,200 on it and its killing me every month

What's more likely to actually help: a balance transfer card with a 0% intro APR (many run 15–21 months), or a personal loan at a lower rate to pay it off in a fixed timeline. Both let you stop the bleeding while you pay it down. The bank's answer being "no" twice doesn't mean your options are exhausted — it just means the option that required the least effort on your part is closed.
